nameStory: Red trillium gets its name from its deep red to burgundy flowers that emerge in early spring. It's also called "wake robin" because, like the European robin's red breast announcing spring's arrival, this plant's colorful blooms herald the end of winter in New England's forests.
description: Red trillium is a distinctive woodland wildflower that grows 8-16 inches tall from a thick underground stem. Everything about this plant comes in threes - three broad leaves arranged in a whorl, and a single three-petaled flower that sits above them on a short stalk. The deep red to maroon flower (occasionally pink or even white) appears in late spring before the forest canopy fully leafs out, making it a classic spring ephemeral.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Single flower with three pointed petals in deep red, maroon, or burgundy (rarely pink or white), sitting on a short stalk above the leaves. The flower has an unpleasant musky odor that some compare to wet dog or rotting meat.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Exactly three broad, oval leaves arranged in a perfect whorl (circle) around the stem. Each leaf is 3-6 inches long with prominent parallel veins and feels smooth with a slightly waxy texture.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Single unbranched stem rises 8-16 inches from the ground, topped by the three-leaf whorl with the flower emerging from the center on its own short stalk.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Develops a six-angled red berry about an inch across that sits prominently above the leaves in summer and early fall.

habitat: Red trillium thrives in rich, moist deciduous and mixed forests with deep, well-drained soil high in organic matter. Look for it on slopes, in ravines, and along stream banks where leaf litter has accumulated, often growing alongside other spring wildflowers like bloodroot and wild ginger.

seasonality.spring: Flowers bloom from late April through May, appearing just as tree leaves are emerging. The distinctive musky scent is strongest during peak bloom.
seasonality.summer: After flowers fade, the three leaves remain green and photosynthetic, and red berries develop where flowers once were.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn yellow before dying back, and bright red berries are conspicuous until animals eat them or they drop.
seasonality.winter: Plant disappears completely underground, leaving no trace above soil surface.

funFact: Red trillium's foul smell isn't a mistake - it's specifically designed to attract flies and beetles that normally visit rotting meat, tricking them into pollinating the flower while they search for a place to lay their eggs!
confusionNotes: The "everything in threes" pattern makes red trillium nearly impossible to confuse with other plants. The closest look-alikes are other trillium species, but red trillium's dark-colored, bad-smelling flower sitting on a stalk above the leaves is distinctive from the white or pale pink flowers of other species.
contextualKnowledge: Red trillium has many colorful folk names including "stinking benjamin," "birthroot," and "bethroot." Despite the unpleasant smell, it was historically used in herbal medicine, though it should never be harvested as it can take 7-10 years for a plant to mature enough to flower.
compareHints: Red trillium is easily distinguished from other New England trilliums by its dark red flower color and strong musky odor. Large white trillium has pure white flowers, painted trillium has white petals with pink stripes, and nodding trillium's flower hangs down below the leaves rather than sitting above them.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Painted trillium is the only New England trillium with distinctly wavy petal edges and painted pink or red markings on white petals.
Among New England trilliums, large white trillium stands out with its pure white, upward-facing flowers that are notably larger than the others.
Unlike red trillium which holds its flower upright and often has a musky scent, nodding trillium's flower always droops downward and lacks strong odor.

Little Sweet Betsy differs from other New England trilliums by having flowers that sit directly on the leaves without stalks (sessile), while Red Trillium, Painted Trillium, and Large White Trillium all have flowers on stalks above the leaves.
Bashful wakerobin differs from other New England trilliums primarily by its drooping flower and extreme rarity in the region.
Yellow wakerobin stands out dramatically from other New England trilliums due to its bright yellow petals and sessile flower that sits directly on the leaves.
Prairie trillium differs from other New England trilliums by having its flower sit directly on the leaves without a stalk, and by having sepals that curve backward dramatically.
